rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about baseline performance for any modality, encoder, or profile setting. The most critical uncertainty is the absolute performance scale of the primary modality (RNA) under the simplest, most standard configuration. 2) What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA-2000) establishes the simplest possible RNA baseline. It isolates the contribution of the RNA modality with a fast, well-understood linear representation and no aggregation or fusion complexity, giving a clean reference point against which all later RNA-encoder choices (scvi, scgpt), profile settings (multiprofile + aggregation), and multimodal fusion can be measured. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first run should be the fastest to execute and the most informative as a calibration anchor. PCA-2000 with a single profile is computationally cheap, minimizes confounding variables, and directly answers 'how well does the primary modality perform at baseline?'—information needed before investing in more expensive image or multimodal runs. It also serves as the control for every subsequent RNA-encoder comparison (configs 004, 007) and profile-setting comparison (configs 002, 003), making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice at this stage.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), so evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical open question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-axis comparison: it mirrors config_001's simplicity (single profile, no aggregation, no fusion) while swapping the modality. This establishes the image-only baseline, which is essential before interpreting any multimodal result—without it, we cannot tell whether a multimodal configuration is genuinely benefiting from fusion or simply performing at the RNA-only level. It also isolates the effect of the image encoder (ResNet50) without confounding from aggregation or fusion choices. Under a tight budget, securing both unimodal baselines before testing fusion is the highest-information-per-experiment strategy.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA-2000) achieves 48.5% acc / 46.4% F1, while config_010 (image-only, singleprofile, ResNet50) is very weak at 20.8% acc. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, and the PCA encoder is a simple linear baseline. Uncertainty: We do not know whether a learned nonlinear RNA encoder (scVI, 200-dim latent) can meaningfully improve over PCA, which is a fundamental representation question that will affect all downstream multimodal decisions. This experiment (config_004: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) isolates exactly one variable—RNA encoder—against the config_001 baseline, keeping profile setting and modality identical. If scVI substantially outperforms PCA, it justifies investing budget in scVI-based multimodal configs; if not, PCA remains the efficient choice and we can redirect exploration toward profile/aggregation or image-side improvements. Under a tight budget, this clean A/B comparison on the strongest modality maximizes information gained per experiment.

Evidence: config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) achieved 0.520 acc vs config_001 (pca_n2000, singleprofile) at 0.485, showing learned RNA representations beat linear ones. config_010 (resnet50 image-only) at 0.208 confirms image is currently weak. Uncertainty: We have not yet tested scgpt, a third learned RNA encoder, and the encoder choice is foundational for all subsequent multiprofile and multimodal experiments. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 in the same singleprofile, rna_only setting? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only the RNA encoder changes from config_004). Why this is best: Completing the encoder ranking (pca < scvi vs scgpt) before introducing additional variables (multiprofile, aggregation, fusion) ensures that all future experiments build on the best-known RNA representation. If scgpt is substantially better, it reshapes the entire search strategy; if comparable, it confirms scvi_n200 as the default and we can next isolate the multiprofile/aggregation question with confidence.

Evidence: Among single-profile RNA encoders, scvi_n200 is the clear best (acc=0.520, F1=0.498), outperforming pca_n2000 (0.485) and scgpt (0.411). Image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208), making multimodal fusion with resnet50 risky. We have zero data on multiprofile or aggregation effects. Question: Does moving from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation improve upon the best single-profile RNA result (scvi_n200)? This directly extends our strongest configuration along the profile/aggregation axis while holding the encoder fixed. Why this is best: It isolates the effect of multiprofile+aggregation on the best-known encoder, uses the simplest aggregation as a conservative baseline, and the outcome will gate whether the entire multiprofile branch (including multimodal multiprofile configs) is worth further budget. Testing multimodal now would confound the image-modality weakness with the profile/aggregation question.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is the strongest RNA encoder (0.520 singleprofile vs 0.485 pca, 0.411 scgpt), and switching to multiprofile+avgpool produced a large jump to 0.650 acc (config_005), the best result so far. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether avgpool is the optimal aggregation or whether transformer aggregation could further improve (or degrade) performance. This experiment (config_006: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) isolates the aggregation variable while holding the best-performing encoder and profile setting constant. It is the best use of the next budget slot because (1) it directly extends the strongest evidence by testing a logical single-variable change, (2) the answer will inform whether avgpool or transformer should be used in all subsequent multimodal experiments, and (3) it avoids confounding by not changing encoder, profile, or modality simultaneously.

Evidence: The largest gain so far comes from switching to multi-profile with scVI_n200 (0.520→0.650, +13 pts), while PCA_n2000 single-profile scores 0.485 and scGPT single-profile scores 0.411. Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) shows negligible difference with scVI. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the multi-profile gain is a general property of having more biological profiles (i.e., more information per cell) or is specific to scVI's learned latent representation. This experiment (PCA_n2000, multi-profile, avgpool) fills in the encoder×profile 2×2 grid: if PCA also jumps substantially, the gain is profile-driven and any encoder benefits; if PCA shows little improvement, the gain is representation-specific to scVI. This cleanly isolates one variable (encoder) against the already-established multi-profile setting, making it the most informative single experiment under budget constraints before committing to multimodal or alternative encoders.

Evidence: RNA-only scvi_n200 with multiprofile + transformer (config_006) is our best result at 0.653 acc, while image-only resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208 acc. The critical open question is whether multimodal fusion adds value or merely injects noise from the weak image branch. Config_032 takes our best-validated RNA pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) and adds the simplest image component (resnet50, concat fusion), directly testing whether complementary image signal improves over the RNA-only ceiling. If accuracy exceeds ~0.653, multimodal is a promising direction and we can then optimize the image encoder (ViT-L) and fusion strategy. If it drops below 0.653, it indicates resnet50 image features are net noise, prompting a test of ViT-L before further multimodal investment. This is the highest-information single experiment because it resolves the largest remaining uncertainty—whether the image modality is worth pursuing at all—while exploiting our strongest RNA evidence rather than re-testing lower-priority questions like aggregation for PCA or scgpt in multiprofile.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, concat) is our best result at 0.688 acc, a ~3.5% gain over RNA-only multiprofile (0.653). However, image-only with resnet50 is very poor (0.208 acc), raising the question of whether resnet50 is a bottleneck limiting the image's contribution in fusion. Question: config_038 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings identical to config_032, cleanly isolating the effect of image encoder quality on multimodal performance. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable comparison to our current best, tests a high-impact design decision (whether a stronger image representation unlocks substantially more complementary signal), and the answer will determine whether further investment in image encoder quality is worthwhile or whether the image modality's contribution is fundamentally limited regardless of encoder choice. This is more informative than testing minor architectural variants (e.g., concat vs. weighted fusion) under the current budget constraints.

Evidence: config_038 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat, multiprofile) is the current best at 0.7207 acc, and all multimodal results so far use concat fusion. We have no data on whether weighted fusion could improve or degrade performance relative to concat under the best-known representation settings. Question: config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the fusion-strategy effect with a single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly exploits the strongest evidence (best RNA encoder, best image encoder, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) while testing the one untested design axis at that operating point. A clear win or loss on fusion method will either yield an immediate performance gain or confirm concat suffices, freeing the next budget slot to probe aggregation or image-encoder contribution. This is more informative than, e.g., testing avgpool (already near-equivalent to transformer in RNA-only) or a weaker RNA encoder, both of which have lower expected information gain per experiment.
